components.text: The framework must justify that the asserted moral phenomena require further explanation and that God belongs in the candidate pool.
The framework must justify treating the asserted moral phenomena as explananda and admitting God as a reasonable candidate.
The comparison also needs a sufficiently warranted and non-question-begging conception of objective morality.
The claimed need for a distinctively theistic explanation of moral transformation requires comparison with secular mechanisms.
Moral transformation must receive a comparative explanation rather than merely being listed among the phenomena.
The objection demands a conclusion proportioned to candidate uncertainty, prior plausibility, and the limited comparative evidence.
A secular explanation of one phenomenon limits the breadth and force of any theistic conclusion.
The abductive argument must state what conclusion follows even if its comparative explanatory case succeeds.
A secular mechanism for some transformation does not by itself settle the argument's total evidential contribution.
The affirmative must show that variable guilt tracks objective authoritative duties rather than culture while distinguishing objectivity from goal-relative assessment.
The proposed moral explananda must be specified independently of disputed definitions of objective morality.
The pro account must establish objective moral assessment and not infer it merely from variable experiences of guilt.
A secular theory needs an account of objective moral evaluation among the explanatory candidates.
The variability objection must allow that guilt can remain defeasible evidence of genuine wrongdoing without serving as the entire foundation.
The objection must allow that guilt can be defeasible evidence of wrongdoing without serving as the entire ground of morality.
The authoritative phenomenology of guilt requires an account that distinguishes supernatural authority from empathy and learned moral cognition.
An explanation of apparent authority does not by itself establish the binding categorical duties defined by the affirmative.
The apparent authority expressed through guilt and conscience needs an explanation beyond merely naming its phenomenological character.
A secular account should explain why moral judgments feel authoritative without treating religious commands as foundational.
The demand for an inferential proof of every foundational moral truth should be replaced by assessment of whether some principles are properly basic.
Variable guilt does not determine whether exceptionally obvious moral principles can be rationally basic.
The demand for inferential proof of every foundational moral principle must be replaced by a test of proper basicality.
Objective ethical reasoning requires defensible starting principles as well as factual means-end assessment.
Axiomatic moral starting points require an account of why shared physical creatures could converge on them without divine disclosure.
Shared human needs provide an alternative source for convergent moral attitudes and associated conscience.
Foundational moral axioms need an account of how they generate ethical systems and why agents might converge on them.
A secular candidate should explain moral knowledge through shared creaturely conditions and practical convergence.
A system built from adopted axioms must explain categorical obligations rather than only instrumental reasoning toward chosen ends.
Empathic motivation does not by itself establish that moral requirements bind regardless of an agent's goals.
A coherent system generated from adopted axioms must still explain obligations that bind independently of an agent's chosen ends.
Objective means-end assessment must be distinguished from categorical moral authority.
The categorical-duty challenge requires showing why objective assessment relative to adopted well-being needs additional oughts after the initial commitment.
The distinction between categorical and instrumental oughts remains disputed rather than settled by definition.
The categorical challenge must show why further oughts are required after concern for well-being and an evaluative goal are adopted.
The account must distinguish authoritative categorical prescription from objective assessment relative to a goal.
A well-being or human-flourishing standard must explain moral concern for nonhuman suffering and the agent's character.
Human-benefiting axioms may be too narrow to cover intrinsically significant nonhuman cases.
A well-being account must show that its goal and assessment cover morally relevant beings and consequences beyond human flourishing.
Human-benefiting axioms must account for animal suffering and the moral formation of the acting person.
The conditional well-being account must explain genuinely binding, objective, prescriptive authority rather than only direction toward an adopted goal.
Constructed axioms must account for moral authority rather than merely generating a coherent system.
The secular goal-relative account must explain the binding, prescriptive authority attributed to categorical moral obligations.
The theistic proposal must explain why a loving creator is a relevant candidate for the identified moral authority.
Objective consequence assessment must be distinguished from an explanation of categorical authority.
The loving-creator hypothesis must be demonstrable and add predictive or explanatory content rather than merely naming a further mystery.
Candidate explanations must satisfy methodological standards rather than receiving automatic admission because they are metaphysically possible.
The creator proposal must add demonstrable explanatory or predictive content rather than merely relocating the mystery into an unexplained deity.
The candidate criteria must constrain supernatural explanations rather than admit them solely because they are logically possible.
A divine authority account must explain how people identify the morally perfect deity and reliably access that deity's requirements amid disagreement.
Claims of immediate moral knowledge require a way to handle severe disagreement and confident religious error.
The loving-creator account must explain how people reliably identify the good deity and gain access to that deity's requirements.
Claims of moral access must accommodate historical disagreement and sincere attribution of conflicting requirements to God.
The identification objection requires specifying which conception of God can ground ethics and how moral considerations narrow the candidate field.
A theistic candidate requires discriminating properties rather than an unrestricted appeal to supernatural agency.
The theistic account must identify which conception of God is morally eligible rather than appeal indiscriminately to any deity.
The candidate must be constrained enough to avoid functioning as an arbitrary supernatural explanation.
Even a specified theistic candidate warrants confidence only relative to the depth and quality of the whole explanatory candidate pool.
The bounded conclusion must reflect bad-lot risk and limited understanding, not merely acknowledge generic prior probability.
The qualified abductive conclusion must be proportioned to the depth and quality of the available explanatory candidate pool.
Selecting a refined theistic candidate does not establish that the overall candidate pool is sufficiently complete.
A maximally good creator must explain why consequential moral and religious uncertainty persists when clarification appears available and harm-reducing.
A loving authority account must address why apparently sufficient natural explanations obscure the alleged divine source.
A maximally good creator hypothesis must explain why consequential moral and metaphysical truth remains persistently hidden despite resulting harm.
A loving creator who enables apprehension must be reconciled with apparently sufficient natural explanations and unresolved disagreement.
The hiddenness objection must consider whether God's relational purposes differ from merely producing bare belief in divine existence.
Relational priorities may explain some hiddenness but do not independently supply reliable moral access.
The hiddenness objection must consider whether divine purposes concern relationship rather than merely producing bare belief in existence.
Distinguishing existence-belief from relationship does not itself establish reliable moral access.
